# t18.2 — Defects found during implementation

Three defects surfaced while implementing D1–D4. Two were found *by* the new controls, which is
the outcome ADR-0007 D7 is written to produce. All three are fixed.

---

## F1 — The allowed-character range permitted the characters it existed to exclude

**Severity: HIGH (latent). Beyond the original scope of this task.**

`CustomInstructionSafetyValidator.ALLOWED_CHAR_RANGE` whitelisted `\u2000-\u206F` — the whole
Unicode *General Punctuation* block — in order to admit typographic marks such as en/em dashes and
curly quotes.

That block contains, in its entirety:

| range | characters |
|---|---|
| `U+200B`–`U+200F` | zero-width space/non-joiner/joiner, LRM, RLM |
| `U+202A`–`U+202E` | bidirectional embedding, override, pop |
| `U+2060`–`U+2064` | word joiner, invisible times/separator/plus |
| `U+2066`–`U+2069` | bidirectional isolates |

These are precisely the invisible and direction-reversing characters a charset restriction on
untrusted instruction text exists to reject. An agent definition could have carried a bidi
override that makes reviewed text render differently to a human than it parses to a machine —
the "Trojan Source" shape — and the check that was supposed to stop it was admitting it by
construction.

**Found by:** `AgentTrustContractBoundaryTest.bidiOverrideRejectedFromRepository`, written as a
routine boundary case for D3. It failed on first run.

**Fixed by** splitting the range into `\u2000-\u200A`, `\u2010-\u2027`, `\u202F-\u205F`. The
legitimate typography is retained (`U+2013` en dash, `U+2014` em dash, `U+2018`–`U+201D` quotes,
`U+2026` ellipsis, `U+203B` ※ and the other Japanese-relevant marks, all of which sit outside the
excluded sub-ranges).

**Regression risk: negligible.** The constant was dead before this task — nothing consulted it —
so narrowing it cannot have broken existing behaviour. It is now live, which is the point.

**Note for security:** this was not in SEC-H1/SEC-H2. It was reachable only because activating
dead code forces you to ask what the code actually does. Worth checking whether any other
whitelist in the codebase was written as a block range.

---

## F2 — SEC-H1 was recreated inside the task that was fixing it

**Severity: HIGH at the time. Caught before it could ship.**

After moving the limit constants into `AgentDefinitionPolicy`, the profiles in
`AgentTrustProfile` were written with literals:

```java
new AgentTrustProfile(16 * 1024, 8 * 1024, 300, true, true);
```

Numerically correct, and completely wrong: `MAX_UNTRUSTED_AGENT_FILE_SIZE` and its siblings still
had **zero** references. The constants were as dead as before, now in a new location, and the
task would have reported SEC-H1 closed.

**Found by:** `AgentPolicyConstantsAreLiveTest`, which failed 6 of 8 and named each constant.

**Fixed by** making both profiles reference `AgentDefinitionPolicy.MAX_*`.

**Why the liveness test scans source text rather than bytecode.** These limits are
`static final int` with constant initialisers — *constant variables* under JLS §4.12.4 — so
`javac` inlines their values and emits **no `Fieldref`**. A classfile scan of a codebase that uses
them everywhere reports zero references. Bytecode analysis is structurally incapable of detecting
this defect. The test therefore greps `.java` files, excluding comment lines and the declaration
itself; counting the declaration is exactly how SEC-H1 stayed hidden. Two self-check tests assert
the scanner returns 0 for a fabricated name and > 0 for a real one, so it cannot pass vacuously.

**No initialisation cycle** is created by `AgentDefinitionPolicy` calling
`AgentTrustProfile.forSource(...)` while `AgentTrustProfile` reads `AgentDefinitionPolicy.MAX_*`:
by the same §4.12.4 property the reads are compiled to literals and trigger no class
initialisation. (`ALLOWED_LANGUAGES` is `Set.of(...)` and is *not* a constant variable —
`AgentTrustProfile` does not reference it, which is what keeps the property true. Noted because a
future edit that adds such a reference would introduce a real cycle.)

---

## F3 — A latent trap in the architecture test, triggered by a record field name

**Severity: MEDIUM (build correctness, not security).**

The full suite failed with:

```
LayerDependencyRulesTest.domainIsFrameworkFree:176 Rule 1 (domain purity)
Violations found:
  dev.logicojp.reviewer.domain.agent.AgentTrustProfile
      -> ines
```

`ines` is not a class. `LayerDependencyRulesTest` scans `Utf8Entry` constant-pool entries with

```java
Pattern.compile("L([a-zA-Z_$][a-zA-Z0-9_$]*(?:/[a-zA-Z_$][a-zA-Z0-9_$]*)*);")
```

to catch annotations and generic signatures, which appear only as UTF-8 descriptors. The package
separator group was `*` — optional — so the pattern also matched unqualified `L…;` runs inside
ordinary string constants.

Every record has such a constant: `javac` bootstraps `equals`/`hashCode`/`toString` through
`ObjectMethods` with a `;`-joined list of component names. For `AgentTrustProfile`, constant-pool
entry #100 is

```
maxFileChars;maxInstructionChars;maxInstructionLines;enforcesCharset;rejectsUnknownFrontmatterKeys
```

in which `Lines;` matches, capturing `ines`.

**The trigger is positional**, which is what makes it dangerous. `PromptContentCompactor$FenceInfo`
has the same hazard (`fence;openingLineEnd`) but its `L`-bearing component is *last*, so there is
no trailing `;` and the regex misses it. Any future field reordering could break the build with a
message naming a class that does not exist.

**Fixed by** requiring at least one package separator (`(?:/…)+`). Framework annotations and
signatures are always package-qualified, so nothing real is lost.

**Detection power was verified, not assumed.** The rule's exemption lists assert *exact* equality,
so a narrowing that hid a genuine violation would make an exemption stale and fail the test. After
the change: Rule 4 still reports `10 violator(s), 10 exempt` — including the 7 Micronaut-generated
`$Definition` beans, which are exactly the annotation-driven dependencies the UTF-8 sweep exists
to find — Rule 3 still `2 violator(s), 2 exempt`, the Rule 8 control still sees its fixture, and
Rule 0 still parses 334/334 classes.

**A compensating guard was added**, `Rule 0b: no class lives in the default package`. The
narrowing is safe only while every class is package-qualified; that assumption is now asserted
rather than assumed, so it cannot decay silently.

Renaming `maxInstructionLines` would also have made the build green. It was rejected: it fixes one
symptom, leaves the trap armed for the next record, and distorts domain vocabulary to satisfy a
regex.

**Architect note:** `LayerDependencyRulesTest` is a structural artifact from an earlier task. The
change is a false-positive fix plus a new guard, not a relaxation, but it is your file to review.
